crafts.name: Kütahya Çinisi
crafts.description:
Glazed tiles and vessels from Kütahya in western Anatolia, a center of ceramic production since at least the 14th century. Kütahya workshops grew in importance in the 17th and 18th centuries, after the decline of İznik.

How it is made
A design drawn on paper is pricked along its lines and charcoal dust is pounced through it onto the white slip. The outlines are drawn in dark paint, the motifs are filled with cobalt blue, turquoise, green, and red, and the piece is covered with a clear glaze and fired in a kiln.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
Tulips, carnations, hyacinths, and rumi scrolls are the usual motifs. Pieces made in the 18th century often show yellow and a freer, more personal drawing style than İznik ware.

Cultural relevance
Kütahya tiles decorate mosques, fountains, and homes across Türkiye, and the craft is still practiced in many family workshops in the city, which also has a museum dedicated to its ceramics.
crafts.author: anatolia

crafts.name: Barro negro pottery
crafts.description:
Black pottery from San Bartolo Coyotepec, a Zapotec town south of the city of Oaxaca, made from a local grey clay.

How it is made
Pieces are shaped by hand, often turning the clay on a pair of plates instead of a wheel. Once partly dry they are polished with a quartz stone and fired at a low temperature in an underground kiln, where the smoke of a reducing fire turns the clay black.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
The glossy black finish comes only from burnishing before firing; no glaze is used. Older, matte pieces were made for carrying water and mezcal. The shiny finish was developed in the 1950s by the potter Doña Rosa Real.

Cultural relevance
Barro negro supports many families in the town and is one of the best known crafts of Oaxaca.
crafts.author: americas

crafts.name: Uşak carpet
crafts.description:
Hand-knotted wool carpets from the region of Uşak in western Anatolia, famous since the 15th century.

How it is made
Wool is spun, dyed with plant dyes such as madder for red and indigo for blue, and knotted row by row on a vertical loom with the symmetrical Turkish knot. Each row is beaten down with a comb and the pile is trimmed with shears.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
The classic designs are the medallion Uşak, with large pointed medallions on a red field, and the star Uşak. Many have a deep red ground with dark blue and yellow details.

Cultural relevance
Uşak carpets were exported to Europe from the 15th to the 17th century and appear in many European paintings of the period, which made them some of the best known Anatolian carpets.
crafts.author: anatolia

crafts.name: Kente cloth
crafts.description:
Woven cloth of the Asante people of Ghana. Bonwire, near Kumasi, is one of the best known weaving towns.

How it is made
Weavers work on narrow horizontal strip looms worked with the feet. Strips about ten centimeters wide are woven with blocks of pattern and then sewn together edge to edge to make a large cloth.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
Each pattern has a name, and many refer to proverbs, history, or people. Colors also carry meaning: gold is often linked with wealth and royalty, green with growth, and red with sacrifice.

Cultural relevance
Kente was once reserved for royalty and is now worn at festivals, weddings, and graduations, and as a sign of African heritage worldwide.
crafts.author: africa

crafts.name: Two Grey Hills rug
crafts.description:
A style of Diné (Navajo) weaving named after the Two Grey Hills trading post near Newcomb in northwestern New Mexico.

How it is made
Weavers card and spin the wool, often very finely, and weave it on an upright loom, pressing each row of weft down with a wooden comb so the warp is fully covered.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
Two Grey Hills rugs use the natural colors of the sheep, white, brown, black, and grey, often blended by carding. They have a central diamond or medallion and a dark border.

Cultural relevance
Weaving is central to Diné life and teaching, and the finest Two Grey Hills pieces are among the most valued Navajo textiles.
crafts.author: americas

photos.caption: Two Grey Hills rug. Photo: Kokopelli-UK, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

crafts.name: Mola
crafts.description:
Panels made by Guna women of the San Blas islands (Guna Yala) of Panama, worn on the front and back of their blouses.

How it is made
Several layers of colored cotton cloth are stacked. The design is cut through the top layers and the cut edges are turned under and sewn with tiny stitches, so the colors below show through. This is called reverse appliqué.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
Designs range from geometric mazes to animals, plants, and scenes of daily life and stories. Fine stitching and many layers show great skill.

Cultural relevance
Molas are part of the everyday dress of Guna women and a strong sign of Guna identity.
crafts.author: americas

photos.alt_text: Red mola panel with layered cloth outlines forming birds and plants
photos.caption: Mola blouse panel, Honolulu Museum of Art. Photo: Hiart, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: Molas by Guna women, Playón Chico. Photo: Kent MacElwee, CC BY 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

crafts.name: Chinchero weaving
crafts.description:
Textiles woven by Quechua women in Chinchero, a town in the Andes above the Sacred Valley near Cusco.

How it is made
Sheep and alpaca wool is spun by hand with a drop spindle and dyed with plants, minerals, and cochineal insects, which give reds and pinks. The cloth is woven on a backstrap or ground loom.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
The tight warp-faced patterns have names, and each community has its own designs, so a weaving shows where it comes from.

Cultural relevance
Weaving cooperatives in Chinchero have revived natural dyeing and older patterns and teach them to young weavers.
crafts.author: americas

photos.caption: A weaver from Chinchero. Photo: La Border, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: Cusco weavers at the 2015 Smithsonian Folklife Festival. Photo: Jarek Tuszyński, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

crafts.name: Bagru block print
crafts.description:
Hand block printed cotton from Bagru, a town near Jaipur in Rajasthan, made by the Chhipa community of printers.

How it is made
Cloth is treated, then printed by hand with carved wooden blocks, using mordants and a resist of clay paste called dabu. Dyeing in natural dyes such as indigo and boiling bring out the colors.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
Bagru prints are known for earthy reds and blacks on a cream or yellowish ground, with floral and geometric motifs.

Cultural relevance
The craft has been passed down in Chhipa families for generations and is protected as a geographical indication.
crafts.author: asia

photos.alt_text: Woman pressing a carved block onto a long cloth laid out on a printing table
photos.caption: Block printing in Bagru. Photo: Anildiggiwal, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: Bagru printed sari, Honolulu Museum of Art. Photo: Hiart, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

crafts.name: Yogyakarta batik
crafts.description:
Wax resist dyed cloth from Yogyakarta, one of the old court cities of central Java.

How it is made
Hot wax is drawn on the cloth with a small spouted tool called a tjanting, or stamped with a copper tjap. The cloth is dyed, and the waxed areas stay undyed. Repeating waxing and dyeing builds up several colors.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
Yogyakarta batik is known for brown, indigo, and white, and for court patterns such as parang (diagonal bands) and kawung, which were once worn only by the royal family.

Cultural relevance
Indonesian batik was inscribed on UNESCO's list of the intangible cultural heritage of humanity in 2009.
crafts.author: asia

photos.alt_text: Woman drawing wax lines on white cloth with a small tool
photos.caption: Drawing batik with a tjanting in Yogyakarta. Photo: CEphoto, Uwe Aranas, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

crafts.name: Bukhara suzani
crafts.description:
Large embroidered hangings and covers from Bukhara, an old city on the Silk Road.

How it is made
The design is drawn on strips of cotton, which are embroidered separately, often by several women, and then sewn together. Silk thread is worked mainly in couching and chain stitches.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
Suzanis show large flowers, rosettes, and vines. The name comes from the Persian word for needle.

Cultural relevance
Suzanis were made as part of a bride's dowry and used to decorate the home and the wedding bed.
crafts.author: asia

photos.alt_text: Large embroidered cloth with rows of red and pink flowers on a cream ground with a border

crafts.name: Shyrdak
crafts.description:
Felt carpets of the Kyrgyz, made in villages such as Kochkor in the Naryn region.

How it is made
Wool is laid out on a reed mat, wetted, and rolled for hours until it becomes felt. Two dyed felts are cut with the same pattern, the pieces are swapped like a puzzle, and they are stitched to a backing with a cord along the seams.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
The mirrored patterns are often horn shapes (kochkor muiuz, the ram's horn) and other motifs of nature and protection.

Cultural relevance
Shyrdaks cover the floor of the yurt. The art of Kyrgyz and Kazakh felt carpets was inscribed by UNESCO in 2012 as needing urgent safeguarding.
crafts.author: asia

photos.caption: Shyrdak. Photo: Firespeaker, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: Kyrgyz shyrdaks. Photo: Ada Awa, CC BY-SA 2.0, Wikimedia Commons

crafts.name: Haida totem pole
crafts.address: Skidegate, Haida Gwaii, British Columbia, Canada
crafts.description:
Monumental poles carved by Haida artists on Haida Gwaii, the islands off the north coast of British Columbia.

How it is made
A single western red cedar log is hollowed at the back and carved with adzes, chisels, and knives. Parts are painted in black, red, and blue-green.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
The figures are family crests, such as Raven, Eagle, Bear, and Killer Whale, stacked from bottom to top, and tell the history and rights of a family or clan.

Cultural relevance
Poles are raised at potlatch ceremonies. Six poles stand in front of the Haida Heritage Centre at Kay Llnagaay near Skidegate.
crafts.author: americas

crafts.name: Ainu embroidered robe
crafts.description:
Robes of the Ainu of Hokkaido, decorated with cut cloth appliqué and embroidery. The Nibutani Ainu Culture Museum in Biratori holds many examples.

How it is made
Shapes of cotton cloth are cut and sewn onto a dark robe, and their lines are then embroidered over, often in chain stitch.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
The patterns are built from moreu, a swirling line, and aiushi, a thorn shape. They are placed around the collar, cuffs, back, and hem, and are traditionally believed to keep evil spirits away from these openings.

Cultural relevance
The skill was passed from mother to daughter, and robes are worn today at ceremonies and dances.

photos.caption: Ainu robe, Nibutani Ainu Culture Museum. Photo: Calistemon, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

crafts.name: Kinngait stone carving
crafts.description:
Stone sculpture from Kinngait (formerly Cape Dorset) on Baffin Island, one of the most famous art communities of the Arctic.

How it is made
Carvers cut the stone, often a green serpentinite, roughly to shape with saws and axes, refine it with rasps and files, and polish it smooth.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
Common subjects are animals of the Arctic, such as bears, owls, and walrus, and figures from Inuit life and stories. The dancing bear is a well known Kinngait theme.

Cultural relevance
The West Baffin Eskimo Co-operative, founded in 1959, brought Kinngait carving and printmaking to galleries around the world.
crafts.author: americas

photos.alt_text: Polished green stone sculpture of two figures facing each other
photos.caption: Legendary figure, Kinngait (Cape Dorset), Honolulu Museum of Art. Photo: Hiart, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

crafts.name: Pounamu carving
crafts.description:
Carved greenstone (pounamu, nephrite jade) from the West Coast of the South Island of Aotearoa New Zealand. Hokitika is known for its pounamu carvers.

How it is made
Pounamu is very hard, so it is cut with diamond saws and ground and polished with wheels and stones. Holes were traditionally drilled with a bow drill and sand.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
Forms include the hei-tiki, the koru (an unfurling fern), the twist, and the toki (adze). Pounamu is often given as a gift, and many believe it should not be bought for oneself.

Cultural relevance
Pounamu is a taonga (treasure) for Māori. Ngāi Tahu are the kaitiaki (guardians) of pounamu on the South Island under the Ngāi Tahu (Pounamu Vesting) Act 1997.
crafts.author: pacific

crafts.name: Eskişehir meerschaum pipe
crafts.description:
Pipes and objects carved from meerschaum (sepiolite), a soft white mineral mined around Eskişehir in central Anatolia.

How it is made
Blocks of meerschaum are soaked in water to soften them, carved with knives and files, drilled, dried, and polished in hot beeswax.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
Pipe bowls are carved as heads, animals, and flowers. With smoking, a meerschaum pipe slowly changes from white to honey and amber.

Cultural relevance
Eskişehir has supplied most of the world's block meerschaum, and carving it is a well known craft of the city.
crafts.author: anatolia

photos.alt_text: White meerschaum pipe bowl carved as a smiling woman's head with flowers in her hair
photos.caption: Carved pipe, Eskişehir Meerschaum Museum. Photo: Dosseman, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

crafts.name: Wajima-nuri lacquerware
crafts.description:
Lacquerware from Wajima on the Noto Peninsula of Ishikawa, known for its strength.

How it is made
Wooden pieces are reinforced with cloth on weak points and coated with many layers of urushi lacquer mixed with jinoko, a powdered earth found near Wajima. Each layer dries and is polished before the next. Decoration is added with maki-e (sprinkled gold) or chinkin (gold pressed into carved lines).
crafts.story:
How to understand it
The deep red and black surfaces come from many thin layers, and a finished piece can take months.

Cultural relevance
Wajima-nuri is an Important Intangible Cultural Property of Japan. Many workshops were damaged in the Noto Peninsula earthquake of January 2024.
crafts.author: asia

photos.caption: Wajima-nuri rice bowl. Photo: yuuki ゆうき(金野裕希), CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

crafts.name: Ebru marbled paper
crafts.description:
The art of marbling paper, practiced in İstanbul since the Ottoman period.

How it is made
Water in a shallow tray is thickened with gum tragacanth. Colors mixed with ox gall are sprinkled onto the surface with horsehair brushes and float. Patterns are drawn with an awl or comb, and a sheet of paper is laid on the water to take up the design.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
Each sheet is unique. Classic patterns include battal (stone), gelgit (back and forth), and flower ebru, invented by Necmeddin Okyay.

Cultural relevance
Marbled paper was used for book covers and calligraphy borders. Turkish ebru was inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2014.
crafts.author: anatolia

photos.alt_text: Marbled paper with a red and green flower inside a yellow circle on a swirled background

photos.caption: Making ebru. Photo: Metasqaure10, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

crafts.name: Hon-minoshi washi
crafts.description:
Handmade paper from Mino in Gifu Prefecture, where paper has been made for more than 1,300 years.

How it is made
The inner bark of the kozo (paper mulberry) is soaked, boiled, cleaned of specks by hand, and beaten into fibers. The fibers are mixed with water and plant mucilage and scooped up on a mesh mould, which is rocked to spread them evenly. The sheets are pressed and dried on boards.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
Hon-minoshi is thin, strong, and even, with long fibers that can be seen when it is held to the light.

Cultural relevance
Washi made in Mino, Hamada, and Ogawa was inscribed on UNESCO's intangible heritage list in 2014. It is used for shoji screens and the repair of books and art.
crafts.author: asia

photos.alt_text: Row of glowing lamps made of washi paper on a dark wall
photos.caption: Washi lamps, Mino Washi Akari Art Hall. Photo: Asturio Cantabrio, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

crafts.name: Hopi coiled plaque
crafts.description:
Coiled plaques and baskets made by Hopi women on Second Mesa in northern Arizona.

How it is made
Thick bundles of galleta grass are coiled and wrapped with strips of yucca leaf, stitch by stitch, using an awl. Yucca is used in its natural colors or dyed.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
Designs include katsina figures, birds, clouds, and whirlwind patterns. Second Mesa is known for coiled work, Third Mesa for wicker.

Cultural relevance
Plaques are given at weddings, ceremonies, and dances, and are an important part of Hopi life.
crafts.author: americas

photos.caption: Hopi coiled meal tray, Chazen Museum of Art. Photo: Daderot, CC0, Wikimedia Commons

crafts.name: Kete
crafts.description:
Bags and baskets plaited from harakeke (New Zealand flax) by Māori weavers. Rotorua is home to Te Wānanga Raranga Whatu, the national weaving school at Te Puia.

How it is made
Leaves are cut following tikanga (customs), split into strips, softened, and sometimes dyed black with mud and plant tannins. The strips are plaited into the body of the kete, and handles are added.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
Kete whakairo have patterns plaited in, with names such as poutama (a stepped pattern of growth and learning).

Cultural relevance
Kete are part of everyday life and of stories: knowledge is said to have come to people in three baskets of knowledge.
crafts.author: pacific

photos.caption: Kete whakairo, National Museum of Ethnology, Osaka. Photo: Yanajin33, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

crafts.name: Ndebele beadwork
crafts.description:
Beadwork of the Ndebele people of South Africa, made in Mpumalanga and nearby regions.

How it is made
Small glass beads are threaded and stitched onto grass or fabric rings, aprons, and blankets.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
Bold geometric patterns in bright colors on a white background, like Ndebele house painting. The kind of item worn shows stages of a woman's life, such as the apron of a married woman.

Cultural relevance
Beadwork and painted houses are some of the best known expressions of Ndebele identity.
crafts.author: africa

photos.caption: Ndebele beaded cape, Dallas Museum of Art. Photo: Mary Harrsch, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: Ndebele beaded apron. Photo: Yanajin33, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

crafts.name: Maasai beadwork
crafts.description:
Collars, earrings, and bracelets made by Maasai women in Kenya and Tanzania. Narok is a market town in Maasai country.

How it is made
Glass beads are strung on wire or thread and sewn onto leather or stiff supports to make flat collars and other pieces.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
Colors are often linked with meanings, such as red with bravery and unity, blue with the sky and water, and green with the land, though meanings differ between communities.

Cultural relevance
Beadwork shows a person's age, status, and life events, and is worn at ceremonies such as weddings.
crafts.author: africa

photos.caption: Maasai beaded collar. Photo: Cecilia Nkini, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: Beadwork in Kajiado County, Kenya. Photo: Mark Myles Mugambi, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

crafts.name: Zuni jewelry
crafts.address: Zuni Pueblo, New Mexico, United States
crafts.description:
Silver jewelry set with small cut stones, made by Zuni artists at Zuni Pueblo in western New Mexico.

How it is made
Turquoise and other stones are cut and ground into tiny pieces, then set one by one in silver bezels soldered onto the piece.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
In needlepoint the stones are long and pointed; in petit point they are small ovals or teardrops. Zuni artists are also known for inlay, where stones are fitted side by side.

Cultural relevance
Jewelry making is a major source of income at Zuni Pueblo, and many families have practiced it for generations.
crafts.author: americas

photos.alt_text: Silver necklace with clusters of small turquoise stones and a horseshoe shaped pendant
photos.caption: Zuni necklace with small set turquoise. Photo: Epolk, CC BY-SA 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

photos.caption: Zuni inlay brooch, 1890s. Photo: Anagoria, CC BY 3.0, Wikimedia Commons

crafts.name: Gaziantep copperware
crafts.description:
Copper trays, pots, and coffee sets hammered and engraved by coppersmiths in Gaziantep, in southeastern Türkiye.

How it is made
Sheets of copper are hammered into shape over stakes, decorated with chasing and engraving tools, and lined with tin so they can be used for food.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
Pieces are decorated with floral and geometric patterns, and the hammer marks are often left visible.

Cultural relevance
The coppersmiths' bazaar (Bakırcılar Çarşısı) in the old city is one of the best known places where the craft is still practiced.
crafts.author: anatolia

photos.alt_text: Round copper plate engraved with fine patterns and writing around the rim
photos.caption: Engraved copper plate, Gaziantep. Photo: Dosseman, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

photos.alt_text: Large engraved copper tray hanging on a stone wall
photos.caption: Engraved copper tray, Gaziantep. Photo: Dosseman, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons

crafts.name: Krofofrom brass casting
crafts.description:
Brass figures cast in Krofofrom, a village of brass casters near Kumasi in Ghana.

How it is made
A model is made in beeswax, covered with clay, and heated so the wax melts out. Molten brass, often from recycled metal, is poured into the space left by the wax, and the mold is broken to free the casting.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
The craft continues the tradition of Akan gold weights, small brass figures used to weigh gold dust, many of which illustrate proverbs.

Cultural relevance
Krofofrom has been a center of Asante brass casting for generations and supplies figures, weights, and jewelry.

crafts.name: Nazar boncuk
crafts.description:
Blue glass eye beads made in the villages of Görece and Kurudere near İzmir.

How it is made
Molten glass from a wood-fired furnace is wound onto an iron rod, then drops of white, light blue, and dark glass are added to form the eye, and the bead is flattened and cooled slowly in ash.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
The dark blue color comes from cobalt. The eye is believed to turn away the evil eye.

Cultural relevance
Nazar beads are hung in homes and cars and given to newborn babies across Türkiye, but only a few masters still make them by hand.

crafts.name: Sámi shoes
crafts.description:
Shoes made of reindeer skin with upturned toes, a part of Sámi duodji (handicraft). Jokkmokk in northern Sweden hosts Ájtte, the Swedish mountain and Sámi museum, and a winter market held since 1605.

How it is made
Reindeer skin from the legs or body is cut and sewn with sinew thread. The shoes are filled with dried sedge grass (shoe grass), which keeps the feet warm and dry, and tied with woven bands.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
The colorful woven shoe bands and the cut of the shoe can show which area the maker comes from.

Cultural relevance
Duodji is a way of passing on Sámi knowledge, and makers can mark genuine Sámi work with the Duodji label.

crafts.name: Lakota parfleche
crafts.address: Pine Ridge, South Dakota, United States
crafts.description:
Folded rawhide cases used by Plains peoples, including the Lakota, to store and carry food, clothing, and belongings.

How it is made
A buffalo or cow hide is staked out, scraped, and dried into hard rawhide. Designs are painted on before the hide is cut and folded like an envelope and tied with thongs.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
Parfleches are painted with bold geometric patterns of triangles, rectangles, and lines. The painting was traditionally women's work.

Cultural relevance
Parfleches were essential on the move between camps, and painted rawhide work continues on reservations such as Pine Ridge.

crafts.name: Morin khuur
crafts.description:
The horse head fiddle, a two-stringed bowed instrument of Mongolia.

How it is made
A trapezoid wooden sound box is joined to a long neck topped with a carved horse head. The two strings and the bow are traditionally made of horse hair, from a stallion and a mare.
crafts.story:
How to understand it
The instrument is played in many styles, often imitating the sounds of horses and the steppe.

Cultural relevance
The morin khuur is a national symbol of Mongolia. Its traditional music was inscribed by UNESCO in 2008.
